live_web_research.page_text: [2610.10808] Controlled Acquisition and Abstention in Three-Channel Score Conflicts Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.10808 (cs) [Submitted on 7 Oct 2026] Title: Controlled Acquisition and Abstention in Three-Channel Score Conflicts Authors: Mengzhe Geng View a PDF of the paper titled Controlled Acquisition and Abstention in Three-Channel Score Conflicts, by Mengzhe Geng View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: When audio, video, and text disagree, accuracy alone does not show whether to acquire another source or abstain. We study these choices in a controlled three-score benchmark: a policy observes two signed scores, may request the third at a cost, and can abstain. The primary reward is mechanism-specific: abstention is correct only for one designated ambiguity mechanism and is penalized under mixed corruption. Matched controls show that a threshold policy matches always-request decisions with fewer requests; its advantage over always-answer fusion depends on the reward assigned to that ambiguity. On a partially held-out synthetic split, the threshold policy reaches 0.789 +/- 0.006 targeted decision accuracy and 0.481 +/- 0.014 utility across 83 seeds. A three-score majority reference reaches 0.626 +/- 0.008 and 0.252 +/- 0.016, but uses more information. In a matched-budget test, a train-only value selector improves utility over no-query and matched-random policies at 10% and 25% budgets, while pair uncertainty has higher utility at every budget. At 50% and 63.7% budgets, the selector lowers utility despite slightly higher non-ambiguous accuracy. If all abstentions are scored incorrect, majority outranks the threshold policy in utility. At a central temporal setting, full-trace controls match the neural models while position perturbations separate them. On held-out-actor emotion clips, eight-frame fusion has opposite-signed accuracy differences for two encoder pairs, with both actor intervals containing zero; matched-request routing gains are small and uncertain. These results separate full-modality accuracy from pre-request selection value and show that selection value depends on budget and the observed-pair ranking. Learn more × License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.10808v1 [cs.LG] 07 Oct 2026 Controlled Acquisition and Abstention in Three-Channel Score Conflicts Mengzhe Geng Affiliation: National Research Council Canada Email: Mengzhe.Geng@nrc-cnrc.gc.ca Abstract When audio, video, and text disagree, accuracy alone does not show whether to acquire another source or abstain. We study these choices in a controlled three-score benchmark: a policy observes two signed scores, may request the third at a cost, and can abstain. The primary reward is mechanism-specific: abstention is correct only for one designated ambiguity mechanism and is penalized under mixed corruption. Matched controls show that a threshold policy matches always-request decisions with fewer requests; its advantage over always-answer fusion depends on the reward assigned to that ambiguity. On a partially held-out synthetic split, the threshold policy reaches 0.789 +/- 0.006 targeted decision accuracy and 0.481 +/- 0.014 utility across 83 seeds. A three-score majority reference reaches 0.626 +/- 0.008 and 0.252 +/- 0.016, but uses more information. In a matched-budget test, a train-only value selector improves utility over no-query and matched-random policies at 10% and 25% budgets, while pair uncertainty has higher utility at every budget. At 50% and 63.7% budgets, the selector lowers utility despite slightly higher non-ambiguous accuracy. If all abstentions are scored incorrect, majority outranks the threshold policy in utility. At a central temporal setting, full-trace controls match the neural models while position perturbations separate them. On held-out-actor emotion clips, eight-frame fusion has opposite-signed accuracy differences for two encoder pairs, with both actor intervals containing zero; matched-request routing gains are small and uncertain. These results separate full-modality accuracy from pre-request selection value and show that selection value depends on budget and the observed-pair ranking. 1 Introduction Audio, video, and text provide complementary evidence, but their combination becomes difficult when one source is corrupted or when the available sources support incompatible explanations. A fusion model that always emits a label hides two operational decisions. It does not say whether a designated missing source is worth acquiring, and it does not say when the observations fail to identify a safe answer. These omissions matter because acquisition, incorrect answers, delays, and abstention can carry different application-dependent costs. Recent multimodal conflict benchmarks make contradiction detection measurable through controlled perturbations and hierarchical tasks ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . Work on modality interference and credibility-aware fusion shows that source reliability varies across examples ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Tenali et al., 2026 ) . Omnimodal benchmarks also expose counterfactual conflicts across several channels ( Mukherjee et al., 2026 ) . Yet a high aggregate accuracy does not specify the value of a missing observation or whether a conflict is identifiable from observations alone. We ask when a third source is worth acquiring, when a conflict should trigger abstention, and whether its value can be predicted before a request. We study three signed scores representing audio, video, and text. A latent binary event generates the scores before corruption modifies one or more sources. A policy observes two scores, requests the third on disagreement or weakness, and answers when two strong scores agree; otherwise it abstains. Policies never receive mechanism labels. Query and non-ambiguous abstention costs make these decisions measurable. Full-modality value denotes the held-out accuracy change with all modalities observed; pre-request value denotes the gain from selecting requests using only previously observed information. Training and evaluation use separately generated samples, with partly held-out corruption mechanisms. 1.1 Contributions First, we define a three-score protocol that separates acquisition from the final answer or abstention decision (Figure 1 ). Matched controls identify when request savings leave final actions unchanged. Second, a common-rule, matched-budget test compares a train-only value selector with pair uncertainty, matched random, and a non-deployable oracle; it shows where a learned ranking helps and where it harms utility. Equal-information temporal controls identify which simulator findings survive matched representations. Third, actor-disjoint media studies separate full-fusion accuracy from selected-request value and show that the results depend on the frozen encoder pair. The evidence supports a controlled decision diagnostic, not a generally superior acquisition policy. The ConflictBench reproduction code and configurations are maintained in the project repository. 1 1 1 Project repository: https://github.com/MENGZHEGENG/audio-video-text-conflicts . Figure 1: The fixed decision rule. The policy requests text when the audio and video signs disagree or either observed score has magnitude below 0.35 0.35 . Without a request, the two strong, agreeing scores determine the answer. After acquisition, the policy answers only when at least two scores have magnitude at least 0.35 0.35 and share a sign; otherwise it abstains. Utility separately charges for a request and for non-ambiguous abstention. 2 Related Work Multimodal learning has traditionally focused on learning a shared representation or combining modality-specific representations ( Baltrušaitis et al., 2019 ) . In conflict settings, this framing is incomplete because the system must reason about whether a source is reliable for the current example. CrossCheck-Bench studies hierarchical image–text contradiction detection in real-world media with controlled perturbations ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . AV-ConfuseBench tests audiovisual confusion created by muting visually present objects ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . EmoMM steers attention over supplied audio, video, and text under emotion conflict and missingness ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . Our study instead prices a request for a missing score and permits abstention. EmoMM evaluates media models; our primary evidence uses generated scalar scores, with bounded frozen-feature media diagnostics. These tasks and evidence differ. Modality-interference work diagnoses misleading channels through perturbations and consistency objectives ( Cai et al., 2025 ) . Credibility-aware fusion estimates instance-level source trust in context ( Tenali et al., 2026 ) . Source weighting addresses answer formation; acquisition and rejection require additional decisions. C 3 PO studies counterfactual conflict across audio, image, video, and text ( Mukherjee et al., 2026 ) . We take a narrower experimental route to make action semantics explicit: a three-score generator, explicit mechanisms, and a partially held-out split. This choice sacrifices media realism in exchange for a clear test of whether a policy uses observations alone and whether its errors arise from mandatory answering, unnecessary requests, or non-identifiability. Selective prediction studies the tradeoff between coverage and predictive risk; SelectiveNet integrates a reject option into a learned model ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019 ) . Active feature acquisition studies purchasing missing information, including generative-surrogate policies ( Li and Oliva, 2021 ) and cost-sensitive decision making ( Li and Oliva, 2025 ) . Probabilistic personalised cascades combine sequential feature acquisition with a rejector that weighs the cost of unobserved features; rejection can trigger another acquisition stage ( Shpakova and Sokolovska, 2021 ) . Active Acquisition for Multimodal Temporal Data (A2MT) selects modalities through time under acquisition costs and shows that non-adaptive controls can match or outperform learned agents ( Kossen et al., 2023 ) . Acquisition Conditioned Oracle provides a general non-greedy formulation based on expected downstream loss reduction ( Valancius et al., 2024 ) . GuessBench studies iterative visual question asking for active reasoning in multimodal large language models ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Our setting fixes two observed scores and one designated unavailable score, and treats a request and terminal abstention as separate decisions. Its distinct evidence is a comparison of action outcomes under specified reward conventions for score conflicts; it does not establish a general acquisition method. Unlike standard selective risk, our synthetic targeted decision accuracy rewards abstention on a designated ambiguity mechanism; the target convention must accompany any comparison. 3 Problem Formulation Each example has a binary latent event y ∈ { 0 , 1 } y\in\{0,1\} and an observation vector x = ( x a , x v , x t ) ∈ ℝ 3 x=(x_{a},x_{v},x_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{3} for audio, video, and text. The protocol retains seven mechanism labels but only six distinct score-level transformations because invert and swap use the same operation. The training and seen labels are clean, invert, swap, and dropout. The partially held-out split includes independently sampled clean cases and introduces mixed, burst, and ambiguity. Ambiguity receives an abstention target. This is a mechanism-specific reward convention, not a general definition of non-identifiability. Mixed and ambiguity both contain positive, negative, and zero-centered scores in random positions. Their positive and negative score distributions have equal variance, so swapping the latent label leaves the observation distribution unchanged: p ⁡ ( x ∣ y = 0 , z ) = p ⁡ ( x ∣ y = 1 , z ) p(x\mid y=0,z)=p(x\mid y=1,z) for both mechanisms. View PDF Review reports Reviewer3 (AI review) October 12, 2026 AI Review (reviewer3.com) Comments (1) 1. Conflicting descriptions of training split corruption mechanisms — Editorial The partially held-out split samples new clean cases, mixed corruption, bursts, and ambiguity; only clean appears in training. Invert and swap implement the same score transformation, giving it twice the sampling Section 4.1 gives contradictory statements regarding which corruption mechanisms are included in the training set. It first states that '[t]raining and seen splits sample clean, invert, swap, and dropout labels with independent seeds' and Section 4.2 reiterates that '[t]he scorer is fitted on the four training mechanisms'. However, the immediately following sentence in Section 4.1 asserts that 'only clean appears in training'. These statements directly contradict each other regarding whether non-clean mechanisms (invert, swap, and dropout) are present during training. xPeerd (AI review) October 12, 2026 AI Review (xPeerd — DAReview) Summary This manuscript, titled Controlled Acquisition and Abstention in Three-Channel Score Conflicts, studies a controlled multimodal decision setting in which a policy initially observes two signed modality scores, may request a third score at a cost, and may abstain under ambiguity. The core contribution is a benchmark and evaluation protocol that separates full-modality performance from pre-request selection value, and that makes abstention reward explicitly mechanism-dependent. The paper’s strongest feature is its unusually careful distinction between “full-modality value” and “pre-request value,” along with repeated demonstrations that a gain from having more modalities does not imply a gain from selectively acquiring them . The main synthetic result is that a threshold policy attains 0.789 ± 0.006 targeted decision accuracy and 0.481 ± 0.014 utility on the partially held-out split, outperforming a learned acquisition policy under the stated reward design . The manuscript is also commendably explicit about several limitations, including reward dependence, simulator-specific temporal findings, and the absence of reliable selective-acquisition gains in natural-media studies . The main weaknesses are conceptual and methodological rather than presentational: the benchmark’s preferred policy is tightly coupled to a bespoke reward construction; some comparisons juxtapose policies with unequal information or different terminal rules; natural-media evidence is weak and often inconclusive; and claims of broader multimodal relevance exceed what the evidence robustly establishes . Potential Major Revisions Clarify the scope of the central claim and reduce overgeneralization from the synthetic benchmark The manuscript’s framing sometimes suggests a broader methodological advance for multimodal acquisition, yet its own evidence is more limited. The abstract states, “These results separate full-modality accuracy from pre-request selection value and show that selection value depends on budget and the observed-pair ranking” . That claim is defensible. However, stronger implied conclusions about practical selective acquisition are not consistently supported by the real-media studies. The appendix explicitly concludes that “None of the media studies establishes a reliable gain from selectively requesting a source” , and the conclusion reiterates that “natural-media acquisition gains, latency, privacy, and perceptual benefit remain unconfirmed” . I think the paper should more sharply define itself as a controlled diagnostic study, not as evidence for generally effective multimodal request policies. Address the reward-design dependence more directly in the main narrative A central concern is that the benchmark may reward adaptation to the authors’ designated preference structure more than robust conflict reasoning. The paper states, “the benchmark rewards rejection only on ambiguity and charges it on mixed” and adds that the two mechanisms “create a statistical cue for this reward preference. Results therefore measure adaptation to that preference, not universal detection of non-identifiability” . This is one of the most important methodological admissions in the manuscript, yet its implications are underemphasized in the main interpretation of results. Because the threshold rule’s apparent superiority depends on this utility specification, the paper should foreground that the policy is optimal only relative to a highly particular operationalization of safety and abstention. As written, readers may overread the threshold policy as intrinsically superior rather than preference-conditioned. Strengthen fairness of comparisons between policies with different information access and action structures Some headline comparisons are not matched in information or action freedom. The paper itself notes, “This is a full-information reference comparison, not a matched acquisition-policy ranking” when comparing threshold to majority on the partially held-out split . It also notes that “the active rule has access to the third coordinate after a request, whereas fixed baselines always receive all three coordinates at the initial decision” and that “A fair real-media comparison would need to define modality availability, request latency, preprocessing cost, and a preregistered encoder set for every method” . Likewise, for the learned acquisition model, “Its no-request branch also changes the terminal answer rule, so this whole-policy comparison cannot isolate the value of its query schedule” . These caveats materially weaken several comparative inferences. The revision should move matched-budget and matched-action comparisons to a more central role and demote unequal comparisons to descriptive context. Reconcile the temporal claims with the equal-information controls The paper initially presents strong temporal-model results, e.g., “temporal gated reaches 0.787 ± 0.006 targeted decision accuracy and 0.574 ± 0.011 utility; the time-mean MLP reaches 0.434 and time-mean majority reaches 0.417” . However, the equal-information follow-up substantially weakens the interpretation: “full-trace template and ridge” both match the temporal networks at the central setting, and “The fixed waveform explains the central and shared-permutation ranking, but the neural advantage under position perturbations remains a simulator-specific finding” . This means the initial temporal section risks overstating representation learning advantages that may actually derive from a fixed positional template. The revision should explicitly restructure this section so that the equal-information control is not an afterthought but the primary interpretive frame. Reassess the empirical value of the natural-media sections or reposition them as negative diagnostics The paper includes CMU-MOSEI, Perception Test, CREMA-D, and AMI evidence, but most of these sections support null or negative conclusions. For Perception Test, “The source-grounding criteria are not met” and “The training pool therefore does not support a source-grounded conflict benchmark under this design” . For CREMA-D, “Each full-fusion and matched-random difference has a 95% actor interval spanning zero, so these results do not establish a reliable full-fusion or selective-acquisition gain” . For AMI, “Neither study establishes a reliable selective-acquisition gain” , and adding modalities can even reduce accuracy, with “audio–video–text accuracy” at 35.77% versus 44.60% for audio–video . These are not flaws if presented as carefully bounded diagnostic failures, but they do weaken any broad empirical narrative. I think the manuscript should explicitly reframe these studies as falsification-oriented stress tests demonstrating how easily apparent multimodal gains fail to translate into deployable selective acquisition. Clarify novelty relative to prior active acquisition literature The manuscript’s conceptual novelty lies in separating full-information value from observable pre-request value and in incorporating abstention into the acquisition framework. That is worthwhile. Still, the paper should sharpen what is genuinely new relative to existing active feature acquisition and multimodal routing work. As written, novelty is somewhat diffused across simulator design, temporal controls, and transfer diagnostics. The introduction says, “We ask when a third source is worth acquiring, when a conflict should trigger abstention, and whether its value can be predicted before a request” . That is clear, but the revision should more directly specify which prior methods fail to distinguish these quantities and why the present benchmark resolves that deficiency better than prior formulations. Anti-fraud / coherence check I do not see strong paper-mill indicators such as incoherent jargon, fabricated references, impossible experimental scales, or internally contradictory claims. In fact, the manuscript is unusually self-critical and repeatedly narrows its claims . That said, one cautionary sign is that many sections depend on numerous bespoke evaluation designs, nonstandard metrics, and simulator-specific mechanisms. This does not indicate fraud, but it does increase the burden of reproducibility and careful claim-bounding. The work fits a coherent ML evaluation paradigm, yet several positive takeaways are much weaker than the paper’s broad framing might initially suggest. Potential Minor Revisions Typographic and stylistic issues The manuscript contains multiple OCR-visible spacing/hyphenation artifacts in section headers and text, such as “M ECHANISM - LEVEL BEHAVIOR,” “NATURAL - MEDIA DIAGNOSTICS,” “W HOLE - POLICY LEARNED ACQUISITION DIAGNOSTIC,” and “C OST SENSITIVITY AND INFORMATION BUDGET” on pages 6, 10, and 8/18-equivalent appendix views . article.body:
Multimodal Paper Explores Decision Policy for Conflicting Scores

Mengzhe Geng's arXiv paper investigates a decision policy for conflicting audio, video, and text scores. The policy, after observing two scores, can either request the third at a cost or abstain. In a partially held-out synthetic test, a threshold policy matched always-request decisions with fewer requests, but the advantage over always-answer fusion depended on the reward assigned to ambiguity.

The paper does not disclose any commercial deals, buyers, customers, or contract values. It reports benchmark performance, not revenue or market adoption.

This research focuses on the decision-making process in a controlled three-score benchmark, where a policy observes two signed scores, may request the third at a cost, and can abstain. The primary reward is mechanism-specific: abstention is correct only for one designated ambiguity mechanism and is penalized under mixed corruption. Matched controls show that a threshold policy matches always-request decisions with fewer requests; its advantage over always-answer fusion depends on the reward assigned to that ambiguity.

On a partially held-out synthetic split, the threshold policy reached 0.789 ± 0.006 targeted decision accuracy and 0.481 ± 0.014 utility across 83 seeds. A three-score majority reference reached 0.626 ± 0.008 and 0.252 ± 0.016, but uses more information.

The study's findings demonstrate that selection value depends on budget and observed-pair ranking rather than accuracy alone. This research contributes to the understanding of multimodal decision-making in situations where multiple sources disagree.
